USA.rationale:
RECOMMENDATION: Continue active negotiations without making new commitments or escalating tariffs. The US holds a position of relative strength — China's economy is deteriorating faster than America's, and talks are in their 'final weeks' per Lighthizer (March 12 testimony). Maintain maximum leverage on structural issues (IP, forced tech transfer, enforcement mechanism) while allowing the negotiation process to conclude. Do not prematurely roll back existing tariffs, which are the primary source of leverage.

SUPPORTING RATIONALE: The US position is moderately favorable (threat_score = -0.3). Evidence: (1) China's Q4 2018 GDP hit a 28-year low of 6.4%, manufacturing PMI contracted below 50 in Dec 2018, and industrial production slowed to 5.7% — the tariffs are biting China harder than the US (Politico, Jan 20; The Diplomat, Feb 2). (2) US economic data shows resilience — the Fed holds rates at 2.41%, manufacturing is still expanding (though slowing), and the labor market remains tight. Tariff costs to the US exist (Tax Foundation estimates $30B+ drag, 94K jobs) but are manageable in a $20T economy. (3) The Huawei indictments (23 charges, Jan 28) provide additional non-tariff leverage that China desperately wants resolved. (4) Trump's Feb 24 delay of the List 3 hike preserved negotiating capital without conceding anything — the tariff threat at 25% on $200B remains suspended, not removed. (5) Six MOUs are being drafted on structural issues (forced tech transfer, IP, services, currency, agriculture, non-tariff barriers), representing the most substantive engagement to date (CNBC, Feb 21). (6) Key risk: enforcement mechanism remains unresolved. China has historically reneged on commitments (NYT, Feb 21). Any deal without automatic snapback provisions would be a strategic loss. The action_score of +0.1 reflects a slight lean toward engagement — talks are producing real framework progress, and premature escalation (raising List 3 to 25%) would collapse negotiations and hurt US farmers and manufacturers already strained by retaliatory tariffs. But this is NOT a concession posture — existing tariffs stay as leverage until structural reforms are locked in with enforceable terms.
key_factors: China GDP at 28-year low (6.4% Q4 2018), manufacturing PMI contracting
US tariffs creating asymmetric pressure — China's export hubs suffering more than US consumers
Huawei indictments provide non-tariff leverage; China wants Meng released
Six MOUs being drafted on structural issues — most substantive progress to date
Enforcement mechanism unresolved — critical to prevent China from reneging
List 3 hike suspended but not removed — tariff threat preserved as leverage
US domestic costs manageable: ~$30B GDP drag, 94K jobs lost vs $20T economy

sources_cited.excerpt: G20 Buenos Aires dinner: Trump and Xi agree to a 90-day negotiation window. Planned Jan 1, 2019 hike of List 3 from 10% to 25% is suspended.
US DOJ unseals fraud and sanctions-related charges against Huawei and Meng; US formally requests Meng's extradition from Canada.
Trump tweets that talks have made substantial progress and further delays the scheduled List 3 hike from 10% to 25%.
The original 90-day tariff-hike deadline passes without an increase (already delayed on Feb 24).

China's economy slows further, matching its lowest-ever quarterly growth. Q4 growth rate of 6.4% — lowest since 1992. Industrial production grew 5.7% in December, up from 5.4% in November, which was the lowest reading since November 2008.

Negotiators are drawing up six memorandums of understanding on structural issues: forced technology transfer and cyber theft, intellectual property rights, services, currency, agriculture and non-tariff barriers to trade.
Lighthizer told Senate Finance Committee that negotiators are 'working more or less continuously' to reach a deal. 'Our hope is that we are in the final weeks of negotiations.'

Chinese have largely reiterated promises to allow foreign car companies and banks freer access to the Chinese market and to increase purchases of American goods. But on structural issues, China has made only vague commitments.

Tax Foundation estimates tariff increases will increase federal revenue by nearly $42 billion annually, but cost the economy over $30 billion in reduced growth and diminish job growth by more than 94,000 jobs.

CHN.rationale:
RECOMMENDATION: Continue engaging actively in trade talks while resisting the one-sided enforcement mechanism the US is demanding. Offer expanded purchase commitments and incremental market access reforms, but hold firm on sovereignty — particularly the US demand for unilateral tariff reimposition rights without Chinese counter-retaliation. Maintain domestic stimulus and accelerate diversification of export markets to reduce US dependency.

SUPPORTING RATIONALE: The threat to China is real but not existential. The timeline shows ~$250B of Chinese exports already subject to US tariffs (Lists 1-3), with the List 3 hike from 10% to 25% only suspended, not cancelled (timeline entry 2019-02-24). China's GDP growth hit a 3-decade low of 6.6% in 2018, manufacturing PMI slipped into contraction, and a UBS survey found 37% of exporters have already shifted some production abroad — structural damage that compounds even if tariffs are rolled back. The Huawei indictments (2019-01-28) and Meng Wanzhou arrest signal the US is pursuing a multi-front strategy beyond tariffs, targeting China's tech champions directly.

However, China retains significant leverage. US 10-year Treasury yields fell from 3.23% (Oct 2018) to 2.61% (Mar 2019), signaling US growth anxiety. US farmers are hurting from Chinese retaliatory tariffs on soybeans and pork — Trump's rural base. The Politico reporting (2019-03-04) shows Trump 'badly wants a deal' to boost stock market returns, which gives China negotiating space. The emerging deal framework (NYT 2019-03-03) centers on purchases rather than the deep structural reforms the US initially demanded — a favorable drift for Beijing.

The key danger is the enforcement mechanism: Lighthizer is pushing for the right to unilaterally reimpose tariffs if China fails to comply, while denying China the right to retaliate. This would create permanent US leverage and effectively constrain China's sovereignty (Politico 2019-03-04, citing Syracuse professor Mary Lovely). Accepting this would be far more damaging long-term than the current tariffs. China should negotiate actively — the deal momentum is real and a partial agreement on purchases + currency + some market access is achievable — but not at the cost of signing away retaliatory rights or accepting Made in China 2025 rollback as a condition. The structural issues (subsidies, forced tech transfer) remain vaguely defined in the draft, which gives China room to make symbolic commitments without substantive concessions.
key_factors: ~$250B of Chinese exports already under US tariffs (10% on List 3); hike to 25% only suspended, not cancelled
China GDP growth at 3-decade low (6.6%); manufacturing PMI in contraction; 37% of exporters shifting production abroad per UBS survey
Huawei indictments and Meng arrest signal multi-front US strategy beyond tariffs
US 10Y yield fell from 3.23% to 2.61% — US growth anxiety gives China negotiating leverage
US enforcement mechanism demand (unilateral tariff rights, no Chinese retaliation) is the critical red line
Trump wants a deal for stock market optics; structural reform language in draft is vague and unenforceable
China's retaliatory tariffs on US farm goods hurting Trump's rural political base
